source.title: Understanding the Failure of Batch Normalization for Transformers in NLP
source.authors: Jiaxi Wang; Ji Wu; Lei Huang

record.file_problem: none; the supplied text contains the full paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: Tests batch normalization in Transformer NLP settings and reports its training and evaluation behavior, extending the normalization comparison beyond the settings named in V6.
record.gate_note: The paper compares BN with LN and RBN across Transformer NLP tasks. The reported task scores and TID measurements do not measure training speed; the IWSLT14 text and Figure 1 explicitly describe BN's training loss as lower and training as faster. Other reported results compare test performance and normalization discrepancy, not the training-speed claim.
record.test_reason: Figure 1 and Section 3.1 directly compare training progress with BN versus LN in an IWSLT14 Transformer. This bears on V6's training-speed component in a new setting, although the measured outcome is training NLL per epoch rather than accuracy or wall-clock speed.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors identify training-inference discrepancy as the leading explanation for BN's poorer Transformer evaluation performance, find that small discrepancy accompanies better performance than LN, and propose RBN to reduce it. RBN matches or exceeds LN in 17 of 20 settings, but cannot fully suppress very large discrepancy. They acknowledge that their discrepancy analyses are empirical and lack theoretical guarantees.
record.recipe_differences: Compares BN, LN, and regularized BN in Transformer NLP tasks; it does not reproduce the listed BN speed comparisons or test the full V6 recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect of BN relative to LN varies by task and dataset: it performs worse on neural machine translation, slightly worse on named entity recognition and text classification, and better on language modeling. Post-Norm versus Pre-Norm settings also yield different scores.

fits_no_version.finding: Replacing BN with LN in ResNet18 on CIFAR-10 reduces reported accuracy by 2 percent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization choice affects endpoint predictive accuracy; this result does not establish training speed.

fits_no_version.finding: RBN reduces intermediate-feature condition numbers relative to LN, sometimes by orders of magnitude, and has smaller Cmax in an IWSLT14 Pre-Norm Transformer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularized batch normalization improves measured feature conditioning relative to layer normalization; these proxies alone do not demonstrate faster training or higher learning-rate tolerance.

record.problems: The paper describes the IWSLT14 training-loss comparison but does not report numeric values or uncertainty for it. Text classification results are averaged over three random seeds, but uncertainty estimates are not given. The paper notes that its TID analyses are almost empirical and lack theoretical guarantees.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted. Table 1 and Table 2 report numerous task-level final performance and TID results, but these do not measure the training-speed behavior named in V6; the speed comparison used for R1 is described in Figure 1 and Section 3.1.

untested.parts: Near-zero training classification error in large convolutional networks, including CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and corrupted or random labels.
Spurious local minima and the effect of extra student neurons in two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems.
Depth-related training degradation, identity shortcuts, and training deep networks without shortcuts or normalization.
Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, orthogonal initialization, and trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, loss recovery, curvature dynamics, edge of stability, and divergence.

Faster accuracy gain, wall-clock acceleration, higher learning-rate tolerance, BN versus no normalization, the named original vision settings, and the Fixup comparison. The direct training-progress comparison here uses BN versus LN and training NLL per epoch.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. Lower validation performance despite better training loss does not challenge V6's training-speed component. Final task scores, TID measurements, and conditioning proxies do not justify additional V6 verdicts.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error from random initialization, CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 and corrupted or random labels.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and spurious minima as width changes.
Plain versus residual network depth, shortcuts, special initializations, and training without normalization.
Initialization, signal propagation, trainable depth, orthogonal weights, and convolution kernels.
Learning-rate stability, curvature, loss recovery, sharpness, and divergence.

The study reports training-speed behavior in Transformer NLP settings, but does not test tolerance to higher learning rates or Fixup; it does not test the listed sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10, or Inception ImageNet settings.

rows.measure: Training NLL loss and training speed
rows.value: TransformerBN training is faster, and its training nll_loss is even smaller than LN's, especially at the beginning; numeric values are figure only.
rows.note: The paper explicitly describes the training comparison; the plotted values are not given numerically in the text.
rows.check: The qualitative result is correct. Locate Basic Observations within Section 3.1, Preliminary. Specify lower training NLL versus epochs; wall-clock acceleration and faster accuracy gain are not measured. Appendix A states that only encoder normalization changes; decoder normalization remains unchanged.

relationships.condition: IWSLT14 German-to-English Transformer with encoder BN versus encoder LN
relationships.reason: R1 shows lower training NLL, especially early, and the authors explicitly report faster training; this supports faster optimization per epoch in this setting.
relationships.display_finding: Encoder batch normalization reduced training negative log-likelihood, especially early, and accelerated training per epoch relative to encoder layer normalization.
